title: Pascal and Object Pascal
subtitle: Niklaus Wirth's teaching language and the Object Pascal of Turbo Pascal, Delphi, Free Pascal and Lazarus: clear, compiled and still building desktop applications today.
description: Pascal was designed by Niklaus Wirth and published in 1970 to teach programming as a clear, systematic discipline. Its readable, strongly typed, block-structured style made it the language of computing classrooms for two decades, and Borland's Turbo Pascal made it a fast, practical tool on personal computers. **Object Pascal**, the language of Delphi and Free Pascal, added units, classes, properties, interfaces, exceptions and generics, and it is still used to build native desktop and cross-platform applications, especially with the Lazarus and Delphi visual designers.

This course teaches **modern Object Pascal** as compiled by Free Pascal 3.2, the current stable release as of late 2026, and points out where Embarcadero Delphi differs. It goes from a first program through types, control flow, procedures, arrays, records, sets and strings, units and pointers, to classes, properties, interfaces, exceptions and generics, and ends with how GUI applications are built in Lazarus and Delphi and a complete command-line project. It assumes the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience: you know what a variable, a loop and a function are. No previous Pascal is needed.

To run the programs, install the Free Pascal compiler from [freepascal.org](https://www.freepascal.org/download.html) (on Debian and Ubuntu, `sudo apt install fpc`), or install [Lazarus](https://www.lazarus-ide.org/), whose installers include Free Pascal and add a full IDE. Embarcadero offers [Delphi](https://www.embarcadero.com/products/delphi), with a free Community Edition under licence conditions. There is no official online playground, but [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/) can compile Pascal in the browser. Every program in this course was compiled and run with Free Pascal 3.2.2.

levels.summary: Classes, properties and interfaces, exceptions and generics, and how Lazarus and Delphi build GUI applications, ending with a complete project.
